  CENTER FOR MISSING &                                           )

         REPLY MEMORANDUM OF LAW IN SUPPORT OF DEFENDANT META
       PLATFORMS, INC.’S MOTION TO DISMISS PLAINTIFF’S FIRST AMENDED
                                COMPLAINT

      I.       INTRODUCTION

           Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc.’s (“Meta”) Motion to Dismiss (“Motion” or “Mot.”)

  established that Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint (“FAC”) should be dismissed because it fails

  to plausibly allege either his 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) (“Section 1985(2)”) or his common law

  conspiracy claims. Plaintiff’s “Protective Opposition1” (“Opposition” or “Opp.”) fails to

  meaningfully contest any of the grounds for dismissal, instead largely re-iterating the vague and

  confusing allegations of a conspiracy from the FAC.

           First, the Opposition fails to identify any specific allegations in the FAC showing that Meta

  and co-Defendants National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) and Katie Hall

  (together the “NCMEC Defendants”) reached an agreement to deter Plaintiff from pursuing his


  1
   Plaintiff styled his Opposition as a “Protective Opposition” because he has also filed a Motion to File a
  Supplemental Complaint. See Dkt. No. 26.

                                                            1

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 39       Filed 08/31/26       Page 2 of 9 PageID# 390




  claims in two other actions brought by Plaintiff against Meta and others. Instead, the Opposition

  confirms that Plaintiff’s conspiracy claims rely solely on the allegations that:

           •   Meta (along with other co-defendants) filed motions to stay discovery in the two other

               actions (Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc. et al., No. 6:26-cv-376 (“Ballentine 2” or

               the “376 Action”) and Ballentine v. Accenture, LLP et al., No.5:26-cv-472 (“Ballentine

               3” or the “286 Action”)); and

           •   One day later, the NCMEC Defendants responded to proposed subpoenas Plaintiff sent

               NCMEC in connection with the 376 and 286 Actions, providing information Plaintiff

               had been seeking from Meta in the underlying actions.

  Nothing in the Opposition explains how these two actions constitute evidence of a conspiracy,

  merely because they coincidentally occurred within a day of each other.

           Second, the Opposition fails to counter Meta’s arguments that the FAC fails to allege the

  “force, intimidation, or threat” or “injury” necessary to state a claim under Section 1985(2).

           Third, the Opposition confirms that the FAC fails to allege an underlying tort to support

  Plaintiff’s common law conspiracy claim. Indeed, the FAC fails to allege any underlying tort, for

  the reasons stated in the NCMEC Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss.

     The FAC should be dismissed with prejudice.

     II.       ARGUMENT

               a. The FAC Fails to State a Claim Under Section 1985(2)

           Meta’s Motion to Dismiss established that the FAC failed to sufficiently allege any of the

  three elements required to state a claim under 42. U.S.C. § 1985(2). See Motion at 8-12. Nothing

  in Plaintiff’s Opposition changes that conclusion.




                                                    2

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD           Document 39        Filed 08/31/26     Page 3 of 9 PageID# 391




                     i. The FAC Fails to Plausibly Allege Any Agreement Between Meta and
                        NCMEC

         Meta’s Motion to Dismiss established that Plaintiff’s Section 1985(2) claim fails because

  Plaintiff fails to allege any facts plausibly suggesting an agreement between Meta and the NCMEC

  Defendants. See Mot. at 8-11. In response, Plaintiff admits that he has not pled any facts showing

  “direct evidence of an express meeting of the minds” but contends he alleged “circumstantial facts”

  sufficient to state a claim. Opp. at 12. But as explained in Meta’s Motion and further refuted

  below—none of the FAC’s alleged “circumstantial facts” plausibly suggest an agreement of any

  kind, much less a conspiracy.

         As set forth in Meta’s Motion to Dismiss, the FAC fails to plausibly allege an agreement

  because the factual allegations relied on by the FAC constitute contradictory conduct by Meta and

  the NCMEC Defendants, inherently inconsistent with an agreement to pursue a common objective.

  See Mot. at 9-10. Plaintiff’s response to this argument is confusing, but the Opposition appears to

  argue that Meta’s and NCMEC’s alleged conduct was not, in fact, contradictory because NCMEC’s

  letters were meant to “displace[]” the discovery Plaintiff sought, arguing that the letters somehow

  constituted “an unsworn and source-free substitution for the subject of imminent examination.”

  Opp. at 8. It is not clear what that means and, in any event, Plaintiff fails to explain how NCMEC’s

  letters (which were never filed or raised in either the 376 Action or the 286 Action) “displaced”

  the discovery he sought from the parties in those actions or somehow constituted a “substitution”

  for the then-upcoming depositions. Indeed, the Motions to Stay Discovery in the 376 and 286

  Actions did not assert that discovery was inappropriate because Plaintiff already had (or would be

  receiving) the information sought. Instead, the Motions to Stay Discovery argued that discovery

  was premature in light of the defendants’ motions to dismiss. See Ballentine 2, Dkt. No. 92;

  Ballentine 3, Dkt. No 49. And, to the extent any of Plaintiff’s claims in Ballentine 2 survive

                                                   3

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD                  Document 39            Filed 08/31/26          Page 4 of 9 PageID# 392




  defendants’ motion to dismiss,2 Plaintiff can again seek the discovery he claims was “displaced”

  or “substituted” by the letters. Accordingly, nothing in the Opposition changes the fact that the

  alleged acts underlying the asserted conspiracy are fundamentally contradictory and do not

  plausibly suggest an agreement. See Mot. at 8-11.3

           Aside from the contradictory nature of the purported conspiracy, the Opposition confirms

  that the FAC relies only on the coincidental timing of Meta’s Motions to Stay Discovery and

  NCMEC’s letters to support his purported conspiracy. Plaintiff attempts to frame his allegations as

  something more substantial by purporting to separate his allegations into “nine numbered

  circumstances.” But, at bottom, all of the “supporting circumstances” amount to nothing more than

  (1) Meta moved to stay discovery prior to imminently noticed depositions and, (2) one day later,

  NCMEC responded to Plaintiff’s proposed subpoenas, despite not yet being required to respond.

  See Opp. at 7-8. Plaintiff’s conclusory assertion that these allegations constitute “factual matter

  that plausibly suggests agreement” is unsupported by the actual factual allegations. Opp. at 8. As

  Meta’s Motion to Dismiss established, the FAC’s conclusory allegations of coincidentally timed

  conduct between two defendants are insufficient to plausibly suggest agreement. See Mot. at 10.

                         ii. The FAC Fails to Allege the Use of Force, Intimidation, or Threats

           Meta’s Motion to Dismiss also established that the FAC fails to allege the use of force,

  intimidation, or threats by Meta or the NCMEC Defendants, which is necessary to state a claim.



  2
    Ballentine 3 has been dismissed. See Mot. at 4-5.
  3
   Although the Opposition takes issue with Meta’s description of the burden to plead agreement for Section 1985
  conspiracy claims (Opp. at 12), courts routinely dismiss such claims at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, recognizing the high
  burden for alleging conspiracy claims under Section 1985. See Caldwell v. Green, 451 F. Supp. 2d 811, 821 (W.D. Va.
  2006) (granting motion to dismiss and recognizing that the “Fourth Circuit noted in Simmons that plaintiffs ‘rarely, if
  ever ... set forth sufficient facts to establish a 1985 conspiracy’ and [] courts frequently grant motions to dismiss for
  these claims.”) (quoting Simmons v. Poe, 47 F.3d 1370, 1377 (4th Cir. 1995)); Davis v. Hudgins, 896 F. Supp. 561,
  571 (E.D. Va. 1995) (“Because of the high threshold that a Plaintiff must meet to establish a prima facie case under
  section 1985, courts often grant motions of dismissal.”).


                                                             4

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 39        Filed 08/31/26      Page 5 of 9 PageID# 393




  Mot at 11-12. In response, Plaintiff concedes that the FAC fails to allege any threats or use of force

  but summarily claims that he has sufficiently pled intimidation. Opp. at 14-15. But as Plaintiff

  admits in his Opposition, his intimidation theory rests solely on the NCMEC Defendants’ allegedly

  premature response to an “Advance Notice of Intended Subpoena” that Plaintiff himself sent. Mot.

  at 11; Opp. at 16. Those alleged facts do not plausibly suggest that anyone was attempting to

  intimidate Plaintiff in any manner, and Plaintiff does not point to any authority suggesting that

  such conduct is sufficient to state claim for intimidation.

         The Opposition’s attempts to distinguish authority cited or referred to in Meta’s Motion are

  unavailing. First, Plaintiff’s attempt to distinguish Scott v. Mountain Mission Sch., Inc. 809 F. 2d

  786, 1987 WL 36169, at *2 (4th Cir. 1987) by asserting that Scott involved “an accusation

  communicated to a third party” while the letters from NCMEC were not shared with anyone else

  is nonsensical. See Opp. at 16. The fact that the letters here were entirely private cuts against any

  intimidation, because absent any intentional publication of the letters, there is no indication that

  the letters were meant to pressure Plaintiff into dropping his claims. Similarly, Plaintiff also

  attempts to distinguish Glynn v. Impact Science & Tech. by asserting that the conduct at issue in

  Glynn (counterclaims raised by defendant) were “litigation conduct,” and Plaintiff contends the

  responses to the proposed subpoenas in the 376 and 286 Actions are somehow not “litigation

  conduct.” Opp. at 17. But Glynn held that the Section 1985(2) claim failed because the defendant

  had “a reasonable basis in fact and law to pursue [the] counterclaims,” precluding a finding of

  improper motive. 807 F. Supp. 2d 391, 422 (D. Md. 2011). Here, the NCMEC Defendants similarly

  had a reasonable basis for sending the letters, because they were responding to proposed subpoenas




                                                    5

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD                 Document 39           Filed 08/31/26         Page 6 of 9 PageID# 394




  from Plaintiff requesting the provided information.4 Plaintiff’s Opposition thus confirms that the

  FAC fails to allege force, intimidation, or threats intended to deter his claims.

                       iii. The FAC Fails to Plead Injury

           Meta’s Motion to Dismiss established that Plaintiff also failed to plead any facts showing

  that the discovery NCMEC provided impacted his ability to testify or pursue his claim, particularly

  because Plaintiff has continued to aggressively litigate both actions. The Opposition merely recites

  the conclusory allegations in the FAC that Plaintiff was “impact[ed]” by his receipt of the letters,

  without identifying any non-conclusory basis for his assertion that this impact “materially

  diminished” his ability to continue pursuing his claims. See Opp. at 18-19. As established in Meta’s

  Motion, such conclusory allegations do not suffice to plead injury. Mot. at 12.

           Neither Haddle v. Garrison, 525 U.S. 121 (1998) nor King v. Rubenstein, 825 F.3d 206 (4th

  Cir. 2016)—Plaintiff’s sole authority for establishing injury—support the sufficiency of Plaintiff’s

  allegations here. In Haddle, the Supreme Court found that plaintiff’s allegations that defendants

  conspired to have him fired (and that he was fired), was sufficient to establish injury. Haddle, 525

  U.S. at 125-26. In King, the plaintiff alleged that he was forced to have surgery on his genitals that,

  among other things, left painful scarring in addition to mental anguish. King, 825 F.3d at 218.

  Neither set of allegations are remotely similar to the allegations here, which consist solely of

  conclusory allegations of emotional distress from receiving information that Plaintiff himself

  requested. Mot. at 12


  4
    In his Opposition, Plaintiff takes issue with the fact that Meta’s Motion to Dismiss sometimes refers to the
  proposed subpoenas simply as “subpoenas,” which Plaintiff asserts improperly treats the proposed subpoenas as an
  “operative request.” Opp. at 5. Whether the proposed subpoenas are treated as operative requests for information or
  merely a notice that Plaintiff intended to make the request operative at a later date is immaterial. The fact remains
  that Plaintiff sent to NCMEC two documents containing a request for information (in the format of a subpoenas) and
  NCMEC responded to those requests. The only logical inference from the receipt of such requests is that Plaintiff is
  interested in receiving the requested information. There was simply no reason for NCMEC to believe, based on the
  face of the proposed subpoenas, that Plaintiff did not want the requested information unless and until Plaintiff
  followed up with formal service.

                                                           6

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD             Document 39       Filed 08/31/26       Page 7 of 9 PageID# 395




         Finally, the Opposition appears to concede that Plaintiff’s Section 1985(2) claim does not

  rely on the “attending court” prong of Section 1985(2), instead relying solely on “Plaintiff’s

  prospective-witness status,” alleging only “a purpose to deter testimony,” not to deter the pursuit

  of his claims. Opp. at 20-21. But Plaintiff has not identified any non-speculative opportunity for

  him to provide testimony in any action. Indeed, in light of the pending motion to dismiss in the

  376 Action (which, if granted, will entirely dispose of Plaintiff’s claims before discovery

  commences), and the fact that Plaintiff’s complaint has already been dismissed in the 286 Action,

  it is likely that no such potential testimony will ever come to fruition. The FAC’s failure to identify

  any actual testimony in federal court that Plaintiff has or likely will offer independently dooms

  Plaintiff’s Section 1985(2) claim.

         B. The FAC Fails to Allege a Common Law Conspiracy Claim

         As explained in Meta’s Motion to Dismiss, Plaintiff’s common law conspiracy claim fails

  for the same reasons as his Section 1985(2) claim: because he fails to allege any non-conclusory

  facts showing an agreement. See Mot. at 13; Opp. at 21.

         Meta’s Motion to Dismiss also established that Plaintiff’s common law conspiracy claim

  fails because the FAC fails to establish the commission of any underlying tort. Mot. at 13-14.

  Plaintiff’s Opposition does not substantively respond to Meta’s argument and instead merely refers

  to his opposition to the NCMEC Defendants’ motion to dismiss. But Plaintiff’s Opposition to

  NCMEC’s motion to dismiss fails to refute the multiple, independent reasons that Plaintiff has

  failed to sufficiently plead a predicate tort as thoroughly explained in NCMEC’s briefing in support

  of its Motion to Dismiss. See Dkt. Nos. 10-11 (the NCMEC Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss).

  Accordingly, Plaintiff does not refute that his failure to plead an underlying tort is independently

  fatal to his conspiracy claim against Meta.



                                                    7

     III.      CONCLUSION

            For the foregoing reasons, Meta respectfully requests that the Court dismiss the FAC with

  prejudice.



  Dated: August 31, 2026
